text: You've read an English sentence up to one hidden character. With yes or no questions, how many do you need on average? The natural answer is five. Each answer halves what's left, and five cuts take 27 to one. The ideal is log base two of 27, 4.75. In 1951, Claude Shannon put the true figure at about one. No compressor beats it on average, And guessing what comes next is how language models are trained. So where do four of every five questions go? Z costs as much as E, yet E turns up 130 times as often. Split the probability, not the alphabet. Is it a space, E, T, A, or O? That's nearly half. E starts near a tenth. Each ideal answer keeps half the probability, so E doubles its share. 3.3 doublings fill the bar. Z, one in every 1260, needs 10.3. A character with probability P needs K questions, where P times 2 to the K equals 1. So 2 to the K equals 1 over P, and K equals log base 2 of 1 over P. Make each character's cost its height. The widths add to 1, so the area is the average cost. Poor the skyline flat, and its height is that average. Shannon called it entropy in bits, one bit per yes or no answer. For English letters, 4.11. That beats 4 but it four times Shannon estimate It ignores what came before What comes after a Q It U 98 of the time U swallows the bar, and the average falls to .16 bits. After TH, E takes two-thirds of the bar and costs about half a question. Half a question sounds impossible, but a compressor asks about runs of letters. Their probabilities multiply, so their costs add. Five questions for these three, not six. After th, it averages 1.7. But averaged over every two-letter context, it's still 2.8. Hundred-letter contexts need more text than any corpus holds, so Shannon asked a person who knows English. His subject read a passage, guessing each next letter until right. 79 of 102 on the first guess. A twin guessing the same way could rebuild the passage from these counts. Treat each count as a symbol. The same skyline. Poured flat sits at about 1.4 bits. That caps the text. More context or a better guesser could only lower it. Shannon's tests with 100 letters of context put English between 0.6 and 1.3 bits. A language model compressed part of a book, posted to Project Gutenberg after the model was trained. It needed 0.84 bits inside that range. The hidden character from the start is the Y in the other day. Shannon's subject needed one guess. Is it Y? Splitting the alphabet took five. In English, almost no letter arrives without a past.
